L9.6: Kidney diagram labeled Cortex, Medulla, Nephron, Renal artery, Renal vein, Ureter.
L9.7: Nephron diagram: Bowman's capsule, Glomerulus, Proximal tubule, Distal tubule, Loop of Henle, Collecting tubule. Glucose and amino acids leave the proximal tubule. Na+ and H2O leave the proximal tubule and the distal tubule. Aldosterone acts at the distal tubule and collecting tubule. ADH acts at the collecting tubule. Na+ and H2O move in the loop of Henle.
L9.12: Thick ascending limb cell diagram. Lumen urine side: Na+, K+ and 2Cl- enter together through one carrier. K+ leaks back to the lumen through a channel, giving a positive potential that drives Mg2+ and Ca2+ reabsorption. Interstitium blood side: Na+/K+ ATPase pump, K+ and Cl- leave.
L9.21: Distal convoluted tubule cell diagram. Lumen urine side: Na+ and Cl- enter together through one transporter; Ca2+ enters through a channel. Interstitium blood side: Na+/K+ ATPase pump, Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, PTH receptor.
L9.30: Collecting tubule diagram. Principal cell: Na+ enters through a luminal channel, K+ leaves through a luminal channel, water enters through water channel molecules controlled by ADH receptor, aldosterone receptor, Na+/K+ ATPase pump on the interstitial side. Intercalated cell: H+ ATPase pump, HCO3- and Cl- exchange.
L9.34: Collecting tubule diagram. Principal cell: Na+ enters through a luminal channel, K+ leaves through a luminal channel, water enters through water channel molecules controlled by ADH receptor, aldosterone receptor, Na+/K+ ATPase pump on the interstitial side. Intercalated cell: H+ ATPase pump, HCO3- and Cl- exchange.
L9.41: Proximal tubule cell diagram. Lumen: HCO3- combines with H+ to form H2CO3, which carbonic anhydrase (CA) converts to CO2 + H2O. Inside the cell CO2 + H2O is converted back by carbonic anhydrase (CA) to H2CO3, giving H+ and HCO3-. Na+ enters in exchange for H+ at the luminal Na+/H+ exchanger. HCO3- leaves on the blood side. Na+/K+ ATPase pump. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors block both CA enzymes (second picture).
L9.49: Heart failure cascade diagram. Heart failure leads to decreased cardiac output. Decreased cardiac output leads to increased venous volume and pressure with congestion and edema, dyspnea and orthopnea; decreased tissue perfusion with weakness and fatigue; neuroendocrine activation with sympathetic nervous system and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system activation; heart rate increase; vasoconstriction with increased afterload; Na+ and H2O retention.
L9.61: Digoxin structure: a lactone ring, a steroid nucleus and three sugar molecules.
L9.62: Digitalis inhibits Na+/K+ ATPase. Intracellular Na+ concentration increases. This increases intracellular Ca2+ concentration by the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger. Fiber shortening (contraction) increases.

L10.7: Sodium channel states. Resting: the channel is closed and Na+ cannot enter; the membrane potential trace sits at rest and rises to threshold. Activated: the channel opens and Na+ flows into the cell; the membrane potential shoots up (rapid depolarization). Inactivated: the h gate plugs the inner mouth of the channel, so Na+ cannot enter while the cell repolarizes. A Recovery arrow runs from inactivated back to resting.
L10.8: Class 1A action potential at -90 mV. Solid line = normal. Dashed line = with drug: slower, lower phase 0 upstroke, lower plateau, and a longer action potential (repolarization ends later).
L10.16: Class 1B action potential at -90 mV. Solid line = normal. Dashed line = with drug: same phase 0 upstroke, repolarization (phase 3) ends earlier, so the action potential is slightly shorter.
L10.20: Class 1C action potential, membrane potential -90 to +30 mV. Solid line = normal. Dashed line = with drug: markedly slower phase 0 upstroke and lower peak; the action potential ends slightly later.
L10.25: Slow-response (pacemaker) cell action potentials, membrane potential -70 to +10 mV. Solid line = normal: phase 4 rises to threshold and a second beat fires. Dashed line = with drug: phase 4 depolarization is flatter (slower), so threshold is reached later and the next beat is delayed. Shaded bars mark each upstroke.
L10.30: Class 3 action potential at -90 mV. Solid line = normal. Dashed line = with drug: same upstroke and plateau, but repolarization (phase 3) is delayed, so the action potential is longer.
L10.37: Slow-response (pacemaker) cell action potentials, membrane potential -70 to +10 mV (same picture as slide 25). Solid line = normal: phase 4 rises to threshold and a second beat fires. Dashed line = with drug: phase 4 depolarization is flatter (slower), so threshold is reached later and the next beat is delayed.

L11.33: Antituberculosis drug targets on Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Isoniazid (1952): Inhibits cell wall synthesis (arrow to the mycolic acid layer). Ethambutol (1961): Inhibits cell wall synthesis (arrow to the arabinogalactan layer). Rifampin (1966): Inhibits RNA synthesis (arrow to RNA polymerase; DNA Coiling, Transcription, and Translation). Pyrazinamide (1952): Exact Target Unclear; Disrupts Plasma Membrane; Disrupts Energy Metabolism (arrows with question marks to the plasma membrane and to ATP synthesis). Cell wall layers labeled: Acyl Lipids, Mycolic Acid, Arabinogalactan, Peptidoglycan, Plasma Membrane.
L11.58: Figure 2-1. The interplay and interaction between airway inflammation and the clinical symptoms and pathophysiology of asthma. Inflammation leads to Airway Hyperresponsiveness and to Airway Obstruction (each arrowed to the other); both lead to Clinical Symptoms.
L11.59: Mast cell mediator release after allergen binds IgE. Granule Content Release (Immediate): Histamine, Proteases, Heparin, TNF. Membrane derived Lipid Mediators (Over minutes): Prostaglandins, Leukotrienes, Platelet activating factor (PAF). Cytokine Production (over hours): Interleukins IL-2, IL-3, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-8, TNF.
L11.60: Early and late asthmatic reaction. FEV1 against time (0 to 8 hours): an Early reaction (FEV1 falls from 100 toward 75 within the first hour, then recovers) and a Late reaction (a second fall over the following hours). Allergen binds IgE on the mast cell, which releases Histamine, Tryptase (and PGD2, LTC4, PAF) acting on airway wall smooth muscle; mast cell and T lymphocyte release IL-4, IL-5, GM-CSF, TNF, TGF; eosinophils (ECP, MBP) and neutrophils (Proteases, PAF) act on the blood vessel and cause cell infiltration.
L11.61: Leukotriene pathway. Arachidonic Acid splits to 5-Lipoxygenase and Cyclooxygenase. 5-Lipoxygenase -> 5-HPETE -> LTA4 -> LTB4 and LTC4; LTC4 -> LTD4 -> LTE4. Cyclooxygenase -> PGG2 -> PGI2, PGF2 alpha, PGE2, TXA2.
L11.65: Classification of Asthma Severity (Youths >=12 years of age and adults). Components of Severity, Impairment. Intermittent: Symptoms <=2 days/week; Nighttime awakenings <=2x/month; Short-acting beta2-agonist use for symptom control <=2 days/week; Interference with normal activity None; Lung function: Normal FEV1 between exacerbations, FEV1 >80% predicted, FEV1/FVC normal. Persistent Mild: Symptoms >2 days/week but not daily; Nighttime awakenings 3-4x/month; Short-acting beta2-agonist use >2 days/week but not >1x/day; Minor limitation; FEV1 >=80% predicted, FEV1/FVC normal. Persistent Moderate: Symptoms Daily; Nighttime awakenings >1x/week but not nightly; Short-acting beta2-agonist use Daily; Some limitation; FEV1 >60% but <80% predicted, FEV1/FVC reduced 5%. Persistent Severe: Symptoms Throughout the day; Nighttime awakenings Often 7x/week; Short-acting beta2-agonist use Several times per day; Extremely limited; FEV1 <60% predicted, FEV1/FVC reduced >5%. Risk: Exacerbations requiring oral systemic corticosteroids 0-1/year (intermittent), >=2/year (persistent). Normal FEV1/FVC: 8-19 yr 85%, 20-39 yr 80%, 40-59 yr 75%, 60-80 yr 70%.
L11.69: Beta-2 receptor signaling in airway smooth muscle. The beta2 receptor couples to Gs, which converts ATP to cAMP; cAMP inhibits MLCK (myosin light chain kinase). Calcium enters through the L-type Calcium Channel and is released from the SR (sarcoplasmic reticulum); Ca++ + Calmodulin -> Ca++-Calmodulin, which activates MLCK; MLCK phosphorylates MLC (myosin light chain); a phosphatase reverses it.
L11.76: Leukotriene pathway. Arachidonic Acid splits to 5-Lipoxygenase and Cyclooxygenase. 5-Lipoxygenase -> 5-HPETE -> LTA4 -> LTB4 and LTC4; LTC4 -> LTD4 -> LTE4. Cyclooxygenase -> PGG2 -> PGI2, PGF2 alpha, PGE2, TXA2.
L11.90: Personalized asthma management: Assess, adjust, review response. Asthma medication options: Adjust treatment up and down for individual patient needs. Preferred controller to prevent exacerbations and control symptoms: Step 1 As-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol; Step 2 Daily low-dose ICS, or as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol; Step 3 Low-dose ICS-LABA; Step 4 Medium-dose ICS-LABA; Step 5 High-dose ICS-LABA, Refer for phenotypic assessment +/- add-on therapy (eg, tiotropium, anti-IgE, anti-IL5/5R, anti-IL4R). Other controller options: Step 1 Low-dose ICS taken whenever SABA is taken; Step 2 Low-dose ICS taken whenever SABA is taken, or LTRA; Step 3 Medium-dose ICS, or low-dose ICS + LTRA; Step 4 High-dose ICS, add-on tiotropium, or add-on LTRA; Step 5 Add low-dose OCS, but consider side effects. Preferred reliever: As-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol. Other reliever option: As-needed SABA.
L11.94: Metered dose inhaler parts: Drug Canister, Plastic Actuator, Spacer, Cap; MDI spacer between the inhaler and its cap.
L11.101: Figure 1. Deterioration in Lung Function in Patients with COPD. Symptoms generally develop only after a significant decline in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) has occurred; they progress as lung function deteriorates further. FEV1 (% of predicted) falls along the Axis of Progression while Symptoms rise from Mild to Severe; Asymptomatic while lung function is normal and while it is first reduced.
